sentence.en: What's your name? - My name is Anna.

hvad koster det?.explanation: "Hvad koster det?" means "How much does it cost?". Say det for things like et hus (a house) and den for things like en bog (a book): hvad koster den? For several things, say hvad koster de? (how much are they?).

sentence.da: **Hvad koster det?** Jeg vil gerne købe det.
sentence.en: How much does it cost? I'd like to buy it.

hvad laver du?.explanation: "Hvad laver du?" means "What are you doing?" and can mean right now or in general (like What do you do?). To ask about someone's job, hvad arbejder du med? (what do you work with?) is clearer. With several people, say hvad laver I? (what are you all doing?).

forms.en: What are you doing at the weekend?

related.en: what are you going to do?

sentence.da: **Hvad laver du** i aften?
sentence.en: What are you doing tonight?

hvad med dig?.explanation: "Hvad med dig?" means "What about you?" and turns a question back to the other person. Use hvad med jer? (what about you all?) for several people. You can put anyone in place of dig, for example hvad med Anna? (what about Anna?).

sentence.da: Jeg har det godt. **Hvad med dig?**
sentence.en: I'm doing well. What about you?

hvad som helst.explanation: "Hvad som helst" means "anything", with no limit. For people, use hvem som helst (anyone).

forms.da: Du kan vælge hvad som helst.

sentence.da: Jeg er sulten og spiser **hvad som helst**.
sentence.en: I am hungry and will eat anything.

hvad så?.explanation: "Hvad så?" means "what's up?" (literally, what then?). It is a casual greeting you use with friends and people you know well, instead of hvordan har du det? (how are you?).

sentence.da: Hej Anna, **hvad så?**
sentence.en: Hi Anna, what's up?

hvedemel.explanation: "Hvedemel" means "wheat flour", the usual flour for baking. It is built from hvede (wheat) and mel (flour), and hvede also appears in hvedebrød (wheat bread).

sentence.da: Jeg bager boller med **hvedemel** og vand.
sentence.en: I bake buns with wheat flour and water.

hvem.explanation: "Hvem" means "who" and asks about a person. Compare Hvad er det? (What is that? - a thing) with Hvem er det? (Who is that? - a person). It also works after small words like med (with): Med hvem skal du rejse? (Who are you traveling with?).

sentence.da: **Hvem** er din lærer?
sentence.en: Who is your teacher?

hvem som helst.explanation: "Hvem som helst" means "anyone" and is about people. For things, use hvad som helst (anything).

forms.da: Hvem som helst kan være med.

sentence.da: I dag kan **hvem som helst** lære at svømme.
sentence.en: Today anyone can learn to swim.

hver.explanation: "Hver" means "each" or "every". Compare hver dag (every day) with hvert år (every year): hver goes with en-words like dag, and hvert goes with et-words like år.

sentence.da: Jeg løber **hver** morgen.
sentence.en: I run every morning.

hver dag.explanation: "Hver dag" means "every day". Hver (each, every) goes with en-words like dag (day); with et-words it becomes hvert, as in hvert år (every year).

sentence.da: Jeg drikker kaffe **hver dag**.
sentence.en: I drink coffee every day.

hverken.explanation: "Hverken" means "neither" and works with eller (or) as a pair: hverken ... eller (neither ... nor).

forms.da: hverken i dag eller i morgen

sentence.da: Jeg vil **hverken** have kaffe eller te.
sentence.en: I want neither coffee nor tea.

hverken…eller.explanation: "Hverken…eller" means "neither…nor" and joins two things in a no: Jeg har hverken tid eller penge (I have neither time nor money). Do not add ikke (not), because hverken already makes it a no.

forms.da: hverken i dag eller i morgen

sentence.da: Kaffe eller te? **Hverken…eller**, tak. Jeg tager vand.
sentence.en: Coffee or tea? Neither, thanks. I will have water.

hvert.explanation: "Hvert" means "each" or "every" and goes before et-words. Before en-words, use hver instead: hver dag (every day), hver bil (each car).

sentence.da: Vi rejser **hvert** år til Sverige.
sentence.en: We travel to Sweden every year.

hvid.explanation: "Hvid" means "white". The h at the start is silent, so the word starts with a v sound.

sentence.da: Sneen er kold og **hvid**.
sentence.en: The snow is cold and white.

hvidløg.explanation: "Hvidløg" means "garlic". It is made of hvid (white) and løg (onion), so it is literally white onion. Garlic is counted in cloves: to fed hvidløg (two cloves of garlic).

sentence.da: **Hvidløg** er hvidt og lugter stærkt.
sentence.en: Garlic is white and smells strong.

hvilke.explanation: "Hvilke" means "which" when you ask about more than one thing. For one thing, use hvilken (en-words) or hvilket (et-words): hvilken bil (which car), hvilket hus (which house).

sentence.da: **Hvilke** sko vil du have?
sentence.en: Which shoes do you want?

hvilken.explanation: "Hvilken" means "which". Compare Hvad vil du have? (What do you want?) with Hvilken bil vil du have? (Which car do you want?): hvad stands alone, while hvilken comes right before the thing you are asking about.

sentence.da: **Hvilken** farve kan du bedst lide?
sentence.en: Which color do you like best?

hvilket.explanation: "Hvilket" means "which" and is used with et-words. With en-words, use hvilken: Hvilken bil? (Which car?).

sentence.da: **Hvilket** hus er dit?
sentence.en: Which house is yours?

hvis.explanation: "Hvis" means "if" and sets a condition. Do not mix it up with om (whether), as in Jeg ved ikke, om han kommer (I don't know whether he is coming).

sentence.da: Jeg bliver hjemme, **hvis** det regner.
sentence.en: I stay home if it rains.

hvis jeg var dig.explanation: "Hvis jeg var dig" means "if I were you" and opens a piece of advice: Hvis jeg var dig, ville jeg ringe til ham (If I were you, I would call him). Danish uses var (was) here, where English uses were.

sentence.da: **Hvis jeg var dig**, ville jeg blive hjemme.
sentence.en: If I were you, I would stay home.

hvor.explanation: "Hvor" means "where". Before a word that describes, it means "how": hvor gammel (how old), hvor meget (how much), hvor mange (how many).

sentence.da: **Hvor** er stationen?
sentence.en: Where is the station?

hvor er toilettet?.explanation: "Hvor er toilettet?" means "Where is the restroom?" It is made of hvor (where), er (is) and toilettet (the toilet). Starting with undskyld (excuse me) makes it polite.

sentence.da: Undskyld, **hvor er toilettet?**
sentence.en: Excuse me, where is the restroom?

hvor gammel er du?.explanation: "Hvor gammel er du?" means "How old are you?" It is made of hvor (how), gammel (old), er (is) and du (you). In the answer, you can leave out gammel: Jeg er tyve år (I am twenty years old).

sentence.da: Anna, **hvor gammel er du?**
sentence.en: Anna, how old are you?

hvor kommer du fra?.explanation: "Hvor kommer du fra?" means "Where are you from?" Literally, it is Where do you come from? You answer Jeg kommer fra England (I come from England). As in English, fra (from) goes at the end of the question.

forms.en: Where do you all come from?

sentence.da: Hej, **hvor kommer du fra?**
sentence.en: Hi, where are you from?

hvor meget koster det?.explanation: "Hvor meget koster det?" means "How much does it cost?" Word by word, it is how much costs it. Hvor meget (how much) works with other verbs too: Hvor meget vejer det? (How much does it weigh?)

forms.en: How much does it cost? (for an en-word thing)

sentence.da: Jeg vil købe brødet. **Hvor meget koster det?**
sentence.en: I want to buy the bread. How much does it cost?

hvor som helst.explanation: "Hvor som helst" means "anywhere", with no limit on the place. Som helst (no matter which) can follow other question words too: hvem som helst (anyone), hvad som helst (anything), hvornår som helst (any time).

forms.da: Du kan bo hvor som helst.

sentence.da: Du kan sidde **hvor som helst** i rummet.
sentence.en: You can sit anywhere in the room.

hvordan.explanation: "Hvordan" means "how" and asks in what way something is done. Before a word like old, much or many, Danish uses hvor instead: Hvor gammel er du? (How old are you?), Hvor mange børn har du? (How many children do you have?).

sentence.da: **Hvordan** kommer jeg til stationen?
sentence.en: How do I get to the station?

hvordan går det?.explanation: "Hvordan går det?" means "How's it going?" A normal answer is Det går godt, tak (It's going well, thanks), and you can ask back with og dig? (and you?).

sentence.da: Hej Anna, **hvordan går det?**
sentence.en: Hi Anna, how's it going?

hvordan har du det?.explanation: "Hvordan har du det?" means "How are you?" Literally, it is how have you it. Answer with Jeg har det godt (I'm doing well) or Fint, tak (Fine, thanks).

sentence.da: Hej Peter! **Hvordan har du det?**
sentence.en: Hi Peter! How are you?

hvorfor.explanation: "Hvorfor" means "why" and asks for a reason. The answer often starts with fordi (because): Hvorfor kommer du ikke? - Fordi jeg er syg. (Why aren't you coming? - Because I am sick.)

sentence.da: **Hvorfor** er du så glad?
sentence.en: Why are you so happy?

hvorfra.explanation: "Hvorfra" means "from where" and asks about a starting point. To ask where someone is going, use hvorhen (where to): Hvorhen skal du? (Where are you going?).

forms.en: Where does the bus come from?

sentence.da: **Hvorfra** kommer din ven?
sentence.en: Where does your friend come from?

hvornår.explanation: "Hvornår" means "when" in a question. In the middle of a sentence, use når for when: Jeg ringer, når jeg kommer hjem (I will call when I get home). For one finished event in the past, use da: Jeg var glad, da du kom (I was happy when you came).

sentence.da: **Hvornår** åbner butikken?
sentence.en: When does the shop open?

hygge.explanation: "Hygge" means "coziness", the warm, relaxed feeling of being together with candles, food and good company.

forms.en: We have a cozy time at home

sentence.da: Vi tænder lys og har **hygge** hjemme.
sentence.en: We light candles and have a cozy time at home.

hyggelig.explanation: "Hyggelig" means "cozy", "pleasant" or "nice". It describes a place, an evening or a person: Han er hyggelig means "He is nice to be around". It comes from hygge (a warm, relaxed, cozy feeling).

sentence.da: Det var en **hyggelig** aften.
sentence.en: It was a cozy evening.

hyggeligt at møde dig.explanation: "Hyggeligt at møde dig" means nice to meet you (literally cozy to meet you). Reply with I lige måde (likewise). For someone you already know, say hyggeligt at se dig (nice to see you).

sentence.da: Jeg hedder Maja. **Hyggeligt at møde dig.**
sentence.en: I'm Maja. Nice to meet you.

hytteost.explanation: "Hytteost" means "cottage cheese", a soft, fresh cheese. It is hytte (cottage) and ost (cheese) joined together, and it is often eaten with fruit.

sentence.da: **Hytteost** er en hvid ost med små klumper.
sentence.en: Cottage cheese is a white cheese with small lumps.

håb.explanation: "Håb" means "hope", the thing you hope for. To say you hope, use håber: Jeg håber, det virker (I hope it works).

sentence.da: Der er stadig **håb** for holdet.
sentence.en: There is still hope for the team.

håndbagage.explanation: "Håndbagage" means "carry-on luggage", what you take with you into the plane cabin. The luggage you hand in at check-in is indchecket bagage (checked luggage).

sentence.da: Jeg har kun **håndbagage** i flyet.
sentence.en: I only have carry-on luggage on the plane.

håndbold.explanation: "Håndbold" means "handball", the team sport. It is made of hånd (hand) and bold (ball). For the sport, you leave out en: Jeg spiller håndbold (I play handball). En håndbold is the ball itself.

sentence.da: **Håndbold** spilles med hænderne og en bold.
sentence.en: Handball is played with the hands and a ball.

hår.explanation: "Hår" means "hair", all the hair on your head or body. One single strand is et hår (a hair).

sentence.da: Hun har langt **hår**.
sentence.en: She has long hair.

hård.explanation: "Hård" means "hard" as in firm, not soft. It can also mean tough: et hårdt job (a tough job). For "hard" meaning "difficult", Danes usually say svær (difficult): en svær opgave (a difficult task).

sentence.da: Stenen er **hård** og kold.
sentence.en: The stone is hard and cold.

høflig.explanation: "Høflig" means "polite", for people and how they behave. Saying tak (thanks) and undskyld (sorry) is polite.

sentence.da: Han er altid **høflig** og siger tak.
sentence.en: He is always polite and says thanks.

høflighed.explanation: "Høflighed" means "politeness", being kind and respectful to others. It is built from høflig (polite), and -hed turns a describing word into the quality itself: fri (free) becomes frihed (freedom).

sentence.da: Han sagde tak af **høflighed**.
sentence.en: He said thanks out of politeness.

høj.explanation: "Høj" means "tall" or "high", for people and for things. Højt also means "loudly": Tal højt means "Speak loudly".

sentence.da: Giraffen er meget **høj**.
sentence.en: The giraffe is very tall.

højlydt.explanation: "Højlydt" means "loud" for noisy people or noisy actions: Hun lo højlydt (She laughed loudly). It is built from høj (high) and lyd (sound).

sentence.da: Det var en **højlydt** fest.
sentence.en: It was a loud party.

højre.explanation: "Højre" means "right", as in the right side or the right hand. For directions, you say til højre (to the right): Drej til højre (Turn right).

sentence.da: Jeg skriver med min **højre** hånd.
sentence.en: I write with my right hand.

høretelefoner.explanation: "Høretelefoner" means "headphones". The word is built from at høre (to hear) and telefon (phone). You wear them to listen without bothering others: Jeg bruger høretelefoner i toget (I use headphones on the train).

sentence.da: Jeg lytter til musik i mine **høretelefoner**.
sentence.en: I listen to music in my headphones.
